stories.headline: Sen. Chris Van Hollen Announces Challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader
stories.summary:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., announced Thursday that he will run for Senate majority leader, becoming the first Democrat to formally challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. Van Hollen, a progressive who has served in the Senate since 2017, posted on X calling for "new leadership." He said voters sent a clear message in the midterm elections that they want "change from the status quo," and framed the vote as a call to "unrig an economy rigged against working people."

The Democratic caucus will vote by secret ballot in a Dec. 1 leadership election, giving grassroots activists nearly three weeks to pressure senators. Schumer has said he has the votes needed to win. Van Hollen's bid follows rising demands within the party for a bolder, more populist agenda after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. Some coverage reported that Van Hollen has accused Schumer of siding with AIPAC.

The Sunrise Movement, a youth climate group, staged a sit-in at Schumer's Washington office Thursday, pushing for new Senate leadership and an end to the filibuster. The group said 54 people were arrested. Right-leaning outlets framed the challenge as evidence of deep divisions in the Democratic Party despite its midterm success, while Democratic-aligned commentators described it as a healthy debate over how to use the new majority.

Democrats are set to retake the Senate majority in January. The leadership contest will shape how the party handles looming fights over government funding and the war in Iran.

stories.headline: FBI Says North Korean Hackers Stole Over $400 Million in Crypto Using Fake Video Calls
stories.summary:
State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency through a scheme the FBI calls FaceStealer, US authorities said Thursday. More than 900 victims have been targeted over the past 18 months. The scheme relies on fake video calls to steal victims' identities and access their devices.

Hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite targets into calls hosted on imposter versions of Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet. They play pre-recorded videos of previous victims known to the target, with audio that appears to malfunction. A message then prompts the victim to click a link to "fix" the audio, which downloads malware that grants access to contacts and apps and widens the pool of victims.

The FBI said the campaign aggressively targets people in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly developers of open-source software. FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman said North Korea relies on large-scale crypto theft to fund its illicit weapons program. Patrick Grandy of the FBI's Los Angeles field office said the scheme exploits trust in common video platforms and personal relationships.

The announcement comes a week after Binance disclosed that hackers using fake job interviews stole a record $6.3 billion from the exchange. US agencies attributed that hack to North Korea-linked actors, which Pyongyang denies.

stories.headline: Update: Zelenskyy Says Starshield Satellite Service Disrupted Again as US Envoys Hold Talks; Senators Demand Probe
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday that his country's military has again experienced significant disruptions to Starshield, the military-grade satellite internet service, hampering its ability to defend itself against Russia. The disruptions were reported hours after an American delegation arrived in Moscow for peace talks. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, President Trump's senior envoys, are holding separate talks with Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Sens. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., and Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., both outgoing, issued a bipartisan statement urging Congress to conduct oversight of the restrictions. They called for accountability from Elon Musk's SpaceX and the Pentagon over the interruptions.

The bipartisan call adds congressional pressure at a sensitive diplomatic moment, as the US pursues negotiations with Moscow and Kyiv. It was not immediately clear what caused the limits or whether they were deliberate. Congressional oversight of the matter would likely begin when the new Congress convenes.

stories.headline: SpaceX to Invest $74 Billion in Data Centers in Texas and Arizona
stories.summary:
Elon Musk's SpaceX announced Thursday that it plans to invest more than $74 billion to build two data centers, one in Texas and one in Arizona. The company is marketing the projects as beneficial to local communities amid growing backlash against such facilities.

In its announcement, SpaceX said the investments would expand local tax bases, generate substantial new revenue for schools and public services, and create jobs. Data center projects across the country have drawn opposition over electricity demand, water use and local costs.

The announcement is among the largest data center commitments reported to date and arrives as the AI buildout drives much of the stock market. A National Review commentary on the news questioned whether activists believe money from blocked projects would simply be reallocated elsewhere, reflecting a view that opposition costs communities investment. Critics of large data centers have argued the facilities strain local resources and offer limited long-term employment.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Says He Would Strike Iran 'With No Hesitation' if Allies or Hormuz Shipping Threatened, as Tehran Weighs Nuclear Treaty Exit
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said Thursday that he would "not hesitate" to launch new military strikes against Iran if Tehran threatens U.S. allies or ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Speaking to Salem News Channel, he answered "No, no hesitation" when asked whether he would use force again, adding, "If I saw things going the other way, I would do that right now."

Trump described the situation as under U.S. control. "We control the Gulf in terms of the Hormuz Strait. We totally control it," he said, adding that "nobody has been killed in the last five months." He claimed the Iranian government is "collapsing," citing what he called 310 percent inflation and unpaid soldiers, and said Tehran's public statements of defiance amount to bravado.

The warning comes as Fox News reports Tehran is weighing withdrawal from the nuclear nonproliferation treaty. It follows earlier Iranian warnings of strikes on U.S. bases beyond the Gulf and reports that Israel ordered stepped-up attack preparations. Trump's remarks also follow his statement that the United States does not need a deal with Iran, and his removal of Vice President JD Vance from the negotiations.

Supporters of the administration's approach argue that a firm deterrent posture and economic pressure are forcing Iran to the brink. Critics, including Vance's allies and many Democrats, argue the war contributed to Republican midterm losses and that a negotiated settlement is preferable to open-ended confrontation. Whether Iran follows through on a treaty exit is the key development to watch.

stories.headline: Update: Attorney General Blanche Says No Criminal Investigations Into Democrats' Oversight Remarks
stories.summary:
Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday that the Justice Department has no active criminal investigations into remarks by Democratic lawmakers about their plans to scrutinize the Trump administration. "There's no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said," he told reporters.

The statement comes days after Blanche suggested that lawmakers attempting to open partisan investigations against the administration could be committing "a crime." Asked what a Democrat had said that crossed a criminal line, he replied, "I'd never said that that point has been crossed." The White House had earlier warned that Democratic oversight plans "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Democrats, who won control of Congress in the midterms and are expected to launch wide-ranging investigations in January, have described the earlier warnings as intimidation of a coequal branch. Administration allies say they are objecting to politically motivated probes rather than legitimate oversight.

A New York Times analysis published Thursday notes that Democratic investigators may face legal obstacles, including the Supreme Court's 2024 immunity ruling, in which Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that Congress cannot act on subjects within the president's "conclusive and preclusive" authority, such as pardons. The administration is also expected to resist document requests and testimony, which could lead to lawsuits over whether Congress has standing to sue the executive branch.

stories.headline: Russian Warship Hit by Ukrainian Drone in Gulf of Finland
stories.summary:
Finnish officials confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday. Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the Naro-Fominsk, a Buyan-M type corvette armed with Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles, as part of a broader drone operation against the Ust-Luga oil export terminal on Russia's Baltic coast.

The strike is thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have hit a Russian ship in a part of the Baltic open to civilian maritime traffic. Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem said the ship was hit around 05:30 local time, smoke rose from it, and it turned back toward St. Petersburg. Damage and casualties are unclear, and there were unconfirmed reports of Russian helicopters destroyed.

Several storage tanks at Ust-Luga are believed to have been hit, with fires visible from Estonia. Herem said one drone briefly entered Estonian airspace from Latvia before heading toward Russia, and NATO aircraft were airborne but did not engage.

Finland's foreign minister, Elina Valtonen, said the Baltic remained stable and safe. Defense officials reportedly told Kyiv that the narrow gulf is used by tankers and carries subsea data cables. Analyst Emil Kastehelmi said the strike was unprecedented in the Baltic but not a serious escalation.

stories.headline: Kalshi Ends Donald Trump Jr.'s Advisory Role Over Polymarket Ties
stories.summary:
Prediction market company Kalshi said Thursday that Donald Trump Jr. is no longer a paid adviser. The company called it a mutual decision that followed his firm, 1789 Capital, increasing its investment in Polymarket, Kalshi's largest competitor, earlier this year.

Kalshi spokesperson Dani Lever said in a statement: "We have mutually agreed to end Don's advisory role after his firm's significant investment in a competitor this past summer." The company added that it was grateful for his contributions.

The announcement comes as Democrats say they plan to investigate the Trump family's business investments once they take control of Congress. Prediction markets have drawn scrutiny over suspected insider trading, including questions from Democratic senators about oil trades ahead of presidential announcements on Iran. Supporters of the industry say the markets provide useful information and are properly regulated, while critics see conflicts of interest when politically connected figures hold stakes.

stories.headline: Brooklyn Apartment Building Collapse Kills 8, Including Two Children
stories.summary:
A three-story apartment building in Brooklyn collapsed Wednesday afternoon at the edge of a construction site, killing at least eight people, including two children, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday. At least 18 people were injured, among them four firefighters. Authorities said late Wednesday that at least seven children were among the injured or dead.

A city official said the building gave way while construction workers were digging at a neighboring lot, and the cause remains under investigation. A deli worker across the street said he heard loud banging at the site all day and saw bricks falling from one of the buildings moments before the collapse. Hairstylists at a nearby salon described a boom followed by smoke and dust as they ran outside.

Torrential rain complicated Thursday's operations, with a pair of excavators scooping rubble as crews searched crevices and debris. "Conditions will get more challenging today with the rain, but operations will continue," Mamdani said. Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said crews had not shifted from rescue to recovery and would treat the site as a rescue operation until they could search beneath the larger debris.

Mamdani said on X that there are "no words for a loss of this magnitude." Investigators are expected to examine the construction work next door and the condition of the collapsed building, and the death toll could rise as the search continues.

stories.headline: Update: Democrat Scott Colom Defeats Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, Becoming State's First Black Senator Since Reconstruction
stories.summary:
Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's Senate race after a prolonged ballot count, the Associated Press projected. He becomes the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Mississippi since 1982 and the state's first Black senator since Hiram Revels in 1881. Mississippi has the largest share of Black residents of any state, and Donald Trump carried it by 22 points two years ago.

The win extends a string of Democratic Senate victories in the midterms, which gave the party majorities in both chambers of Congress, though exact margins remain unclear because some races are not yet projected. Axios reported that votes pushing Colom over the top came heavily from Mississippi Delta communities with a long history of voting-rights struggles. Democrats also won the Kansas governor's race, where state Sen. Cindy Holscher defeated Trump-endorsed Ty Masterson, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Democrats frame the result as evidence of a breakthrough for the party in the Deep South, while analysts note that polls almost uniformly underestimated Democratic strength. Republicans are debating how to recover, with conservative figures including Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts acknowledging strategic missteps, though the party has not broadly challenged the president. Attention now turns to remaining undecided contests, including the Alaska Senate race, and to the incoming Democratic majority's plans for oversight of the administration.

stories.headline: Hegseth Awards Commendation Medal to Sentinel Who Rebuked His Party at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
stories.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday awarded a Joint Service Commendation Medal to Army Specialist Thomas Iglesias, the sentinel who reprimanded Hegseth's group for laughing and talking at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day. The incident was captured on live television and went viral Wednesday, with Iglesias heard calling for quiet and respect at the site in Arlington National Cemetery.

Hegseth hosted members of the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, at the Pentagon and wrote on social media, "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist." The Pentagon said the medal was for Iglesias's execution of his duties.

The episode drew fresh attention to a defense secretary who had survived a House impeachment effort a day earlier, when Republicans blocked it. Critics said the moment damaged Hegseth's carefully cultivated image, while supporters and some conservative outlets portrayed his response as a gracious acknowledgment of military standards.

stories.headline: Treasury Secretary Bessent Moved to Military Base After Iran-Linked Threats, Reports Say
stories.summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Georgetown home in Washington to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports. CBS News, citing a source, said the relocation followed a Wall Street Journal article featuring an online photo that allowed the home to be geo-located, which raised security concerns.

A Treasury spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" and remains committed to pressuring Iran's economy. Bessent has led efforts to isolate Iran through sanctions and a wider economic blockade. The exact nature of the threats is unclear, but Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned in September that Iran had "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, and the New York Times has reported that the effort has reached a more advanced stage.

Several officials already live on military bases, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, and a preliminary June agreement to end the war collapsed within weeks. Other reported Iranian targets include former officials Mike Pompeo, John Bolton and Mark Milley.

stories.headline: Update: Stephen Miller memo shifts Cabinet communications control away from White House, Fox News reports
stories.summary:
A memo circulated within the Trump administration this week describes a new White House hierarchy under chief of staff Stephen Miller, who took over the role on Monday from Susie Wiles, according to an exclusive from Fox News Digital. The memo, sent by Miller's office and titled as a memo on administrative matters and personnel changes, gives Cabinet secretaries more control over their own departments' messaging.

The memo says the White House position of Cabinet Secretary will become Director of Cabinet Relations, focused on supporting and reinforcing the president's Cabinet secretaries. It states that each cabinet leader is the best leader and communicator for their department, and that the new role will make sure Cabinet members are resourced and backed by the White House.

Sources quoted by Fox News said the change reverses what they described as tight, administration-wide communications control under Wiles during the first nearly two years of Trump's second term. One source said the shift would streamline the Cabinet and make it "a more effective instrument for the President, whereas previously it was too constrained." Another said it would let Cabinet members be "captains of their own ship." The account rests on sources favorable to Miller and has been reported only by Fox News so far; critics of the White House have not yet commented on the memo.

The change follows Miller's elevation to chief of staff after the midterm elections, as the administration looks ahead to a Congress in which Democrats are positioned to gain influence and oversight power. How departments use the greater latitude over their messaging is likely to become clearer in coming weeks.

stories.headline: Update: Fresh bomb hoax threats hit about 1,800 Italian schools for second day
stories.summary:
Schools across Italy received bomb threats for a second consecutive day on Thursday, prompting new panic and evacuations. About 1,800 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported a threat similar to the one that caused chaos on Wednesday, although no devices have been found anywhere.

The Italian government has advised schools that, absent concrete evidence beyond receipt of a mass email, buildings should not be evacuated. Wednesday's email went to 6,300 of Italy's 7,476 state schools and was signed by a "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan." Some officials say it originated in Taiwan, while Thursday's message, with the same signature, is said to have been sent from the hacked account of a teacher in the Philippines.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the incidents as "a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern." Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland were targeted on Wednesday, and a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed train services in northern France on Thursday. The incidents follow hoax threats last week against airports and airlines in several European countries; an extremist misogynistic group had claimed some of them but later denied any link, and a Russian extremist group has also denied sending them.

Many Italian parents are demanding clarity. La Repubblica reported protests against a Rome headmaster who took no action after concluding the message contained typos and was fake, with protesters calling for new national guidelines.

stories.headline: Democratic senators press CFTC on suspicious oil trades ahead of Trump Iran announcements
stories.summary:
A group of Democratic senators is pressing the Commodity Futures Trading Commission on its investigation into well-timed oil trades placed ahead of major announcements by President Donald Trump on the Iran war earlier this year, according to Bloomberg.

The senators are seeking details on the status and scope of the probe into the trading, which came before the president's public statements on the conflict. The available reporting does not yet specify who made the trades or how large they were.

The push fits into broader Democratic plans for oversight as the party gains influence after the midterms. The White House has argued that such oversight plans risk crossing into blatant criminality, while Democrats say scrutiny of possible misuse of market-moving information is a core oversight duty. The CFTC has not yet publicly responded in the information available.

stories.headline: Kennedy family members seek to join lawsuit against Trump's proposed Washington triumphal arch
stories.summary:
Several members of the Kennedy family, one of America's most prominent political dynasties, filed on Tuesday to join a court case aimed at stopping President Donald Trump from building a proposed triumphal arch in Washington, Reuters reported.

The filing adds a high-profile voice to litigation challenging the project. The family argues the arch would harm the capital's historic landscape, according to the Reuters summary of the filing.

The administration has promoted the arch as a monument, and supporters see it as a fitting addition to the capital's commemorative architecture. The court has yet to rule on whether the Kennedy family members may intervene.

stories.headline: Shooting in Washington's Logan Circle Leaves Several Wounded, Suspect Barricaded Near White House
stories.summary:
At least four people were shot early Thursday in the Logan Circle neighborhood of Northwest Washington, D.C. Some accounts put the number of wounded at five. The Metropolitan Police Department said the incident near 15th and P Streets NW, about a mile north of the White House, had become a barricade situation in the 1500 block of 15th Street. A police spokesperson described the scene as still active.

Authorities issued a shelter-in-place order covering areas around Logan Circle and Dupont Circle. Residents were told to go inside the nearest building and stay there, and streets were closed amid a large police response. Reports indicated the shooting took place at or outside a Vida Fitness gym, and that an armed assailant had opened fire before being contained in a nearby building. Police had not yet released a motive, the identity of the suspect, or the condition of the wounded.

The Emergency Response Team was on the scene, and a local council member said officers were searching for a suspect. The shooting occurred in a densely populated part of the capital close to federal buildings and the president's residence. Further details on the victims and the suspect are expected as the barricade situation develops.

stories.headline: Update: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns After Affair Revelations Involving Alleged Chinese Spy
stories.summary:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive on Thursday, days after reports of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly believe was a Chinese asset. Huang had apologized on Sunday for the affair with Alice Huang, and a second report alleged a relationship with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Earlier reports said the board was preparing to oust him. Nvidia shares extended their losses after the announcement.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim chief executive while the company considers permanent successors. BBC News reported that several candidates are in the frame. It noted that within days Huang's status as a seemingly untouchable figure in the global AI race had collapsed. Singapore said it held Alice Huang's passport for months after President Trump was reportedly briefed that she was a spy.

The resignation carries political weight as well. Huang was an influential figure in Washington and the Trump administration, and his ties to the president are now under scrutiny. Sen. Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, said Huang should resign, saying he could not believe the company was considering letting him stay. Nvidia is among the world's most valuable companies and central to the AI industry, so questions about its leadership and any national security implications are likely to continue.

stories.headline: Trump Says US Does Not Need Iran Deal, Redirects Vance to Domestic Corruption Probes
stories.summary:
President Trump said Thursday that the United States does not need a deal with Iran. In a Truth Social post, he directed Vice President JD Vance to give his complete and total attention to alleged corruption in Democratic-run cities and states. The post said Vance would not lead face-to-face peace talks with Tehran. Oil prices surged and stocks fell after the post, according to reports.

The move follows the midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered heavy losses. Axios reported that Vance concluded the Iran war was a major driver of the defeat. Trump said at Arlington National Cemetery on Veterans Day that the conflict would end soon and promised total victory. Trump has said the war, which began with announced major combat operations on Feb. 28, has been won, while Iran continues to hold to its demands and to attack ships.

Democrats are already planning oversight. Incoming House Oversight chair Rep. Robert Garcia has promised sweeping investigations, and White House counsel Will Scharf warned that such probes may cross the line into blatant criminality. Garcia responded that the Constitution gives Congress latitude to investigate. Democrats such as Rep. Ro Khanna argue accountability for the Iran war would lower prices, while the White House frames Democratic oversight and Democratic-run jurisdictions as the targets of corruption concerns.

stories.headline: MSF Warns Hundreds of Millions in Ebola Funding Not Reaching Responders in DR Congo
stories.summary:
Doctors Without Borders (MSF) warned that hundreds of millions of dollars meant to fight Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo are not reaching the intended recipients. In a new report, the charity said the outbreak remains out of control. Frontline workers are going unpaid and lack training and supplies, and in some cases ambulances have run out of fuel.

More than 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected since the outbreak was declared in May, making it the second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record. MSF cited surveillance teams that exist on paper but are nowhere to be seen on the ground. It said two-thirds of deaths are occurring in communities rather than treatment centers. British epidemiologist Neil Ferguson estimates more than half of cases are going undetected, suggesting the outbreak could last another year.

The warning follows concerns raised last month by Africa CDC, which said $700 million of $962 million disbursed to response organizations was unaccounted for. Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya called it a major transparency and reporting failure rather than embezzlement. MSF urged the Congolese government and UN agencies to strengthen oversight and accountability, and said North Kivu response has been too slow while Haut-Uele is dramatically overlooked. The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.

stories.headline: Israeli strike on Gaza's Nasser hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
stories.summary:
An Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital, the largest medical facility in the southern Gaza Strip, killed at least six people and injured about 20 overnight, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. Eyewitnesses told the BBC that a single missile fired from a warplane struck a five-storey building housing surgical wards and intensive care units. The ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were among the dead, including surgeon Dr Rizk Abu Shaira, and condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions."

The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who it said used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on Israeli forces. Israel has long accused Hamas of exploiting civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, to store weapons and run command rooms, which Hamas denies. Hamas said Israel was spreading "false narratives" in an attempt to cover up a "new war crime." Israel bars international news organisations from Gaza, so the competing claims could not be independently verified.

Hospitals have protected status under international law but have been repeatedly hit during the war. Nasser hospital was struck twice in August 2025, killing at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers. Israeli strikes have continued despite the ceasefire agreement of October last year, and the health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable, says more than 1,620 people have been killed since then. Each side accuses the other of violating the truce.

The strike comes as conditions in Gaza deteriorate further, with heavy rains reportedly flooding tens of thousands of tents sheltering displaced families.

stories.headline: Biden says he would not have sought second term had he known he had cancer
stories.summary:
Former President Joe Biden said he did not know he had cancer while in office and would not have run for a second term had he been diagnosed. In an interview with People magazine ahead of the release of his White House memoir, Biden said, "If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would've not gone forward." He added that he does not think "an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running" for president.

Biden was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office in 2025, and his son Hunter said in August that the cancer had spread and was causing pain. Biden, who turns 84 on Nov. 20, defended his record, saying age was not disqualifying and that he was "the best-equipped person to do the job." He downplayed his disastrous June 2024 debate against Donald Trump, saying he expected another debate and did not consider it consequential, though it accelerated Democratic concerns about his age. He ended his campaign within weeks and endorsed Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump.

Biden also defended his pardon of Hunter Biden, saying Trump's "penchant for vengeance" made it necessary and that he pardoned family members and others who had dealt with him to shield them from retaliation. Hunter Biden has said the pardon damaged his father's legacy. Republicans have long argued Biden's age and fitness were concealed from the public, while Biden's allies say he performed his duties capably. The memoir, which also says Trump should carry the weight of the Jan. 6 riots, is due out Tuesday.

stories.headline: Ukrainians endure rolling blackouts as Russia intensifies strikes on power grid
stories.summary:
Ukrainians are facing rolling planned power cuts as intensified Russian attacks batter the country's energy grid, even as US envoys prepare to meet the Russian and Ukrainian leaders on Thursday. The outages began earlier this year than last winter and are already lasting longer. In Kyiv, some families report outages of up to 20 hours a day, and one resident described getting only two hours of electricity followed by eight without.

Officials worry life could become unsustainable for millions of people if supply cannot be maintained for at least four hours a day, and some warn privately that the threshold is close. Kyiv has been hit hardest, with metro trains and trolleybuses at times brought to a standstill, and hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians nationwide have lost power in recent weeks. Without electricity, lifts, water pumps, heating and internet fail, leaving residents in cold, dark apartments as temperatures fall.

The BBC visited one of Ukraine's largest power stations, which it was asked not to name for security reasons, and found it reduced to twisted metal and broken pipes after a recent ballistic missile strike described as the most powerful of Russia's campaign against energy targets. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries. The pressure on civilians adds urgency to the diplomatic track, which has included talks in Abu Dhabi and an agreed prisoner exchange.

stories.headline: Driver accused of DUI in Los Angeles crash that killed three pedestrians
stories.summary:
The driver of a minivan that slammed into sidewalk vendors and pedestrians outside the North Hollywood Metro station in Los Angeles was allegedly driving under the influence and has been arrested on murder counts, police said Wednesday. Ihor Demianenko, 61, is accused of crashing into people around 5:55 p.m. Tuesday at Lankershim and Chandler boulevards. Three women between 40 and 60 were killed, and two other women, aged 50 to 55, remain in critical condition.

Police said the impact sent pedestrians and debris flying. Council member Adrin Nazarian said the driver was under the influence of alcohol and veered to the right off the road before striking people on the sidewalk. The LAPD initially said the driver was critically hurt but later said his injuries were minor. His bail was set at more than $6 million, and it was unclear whether he had an attorney.

Mayor Karen Bass said she was heartbroken for the families, while Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, who defeated Bass in last week's election, said the loss of street vendors who had served the community for years was especially devastating. A witness described one of the victims as a fixture of the neighborhood who worked the same corner every day.
